skills.whatItOffersHere:
A complete, written directing method for code-rendered films whose core idea matches this project exactly: the picture is a pure function of time, the look is proven on stills made by the real drawing code, a human approves the still, then motion is added, then the film is reviewed on contact sheets and 0.2 s strips. Everything useful can be READ from C:/Users/RTX4070TI/lemo-opuscar/*.md without running anything.

methodSteps: 1. WHAT A STYLE FRAME IS: a still of an actual shot of the film at final size (1920x1080, device scale 1), produced by the film's own render(t) code. The one rule that defines it, DIRECTOR.md:61: "Render them with the real drawing code, not a mock-up". It is not a Figma/SVG mock and not a generated image. A film without characters needs three style frames, one of them the signature shot (DIRECTOR.md:59); with characters, a model sheet plus two style frames (:58). In the own-style flow a single frame is enough (MY-STYLES.md:101).

2. BEFORE DRAWING: fix the invariants in writing. A STYLE.md with the 11 sections (essence and what it is not, materials and rendering, colour logic as rules not just a palette, motion quality, pitfalls...) and a benchmark note listing what to learn from the reference and what not to take (DIRECTOR.md:26-33). For this job the benchmark notes already exist in REFERENCES.md (Motion film strengths + weaknesses to avoid) and the treatment (scenes, shots, camera, timings) is fixed by the original, so only the look rules are new.

3. PLAN CHANGES AS A TABLE: CHANGES.md, one row per decision - section, base value, new value, why (MY-STYLES.md:19). At most five changes per round because more are hard to judge (:82). Translate vague wishes into explicit options, never silent edits (:69-76). Changes that travel together must be checked together, e.g. faster motion needs more going on, a darker palette needs type contrast re-checked (:81). Summarise and wait for the owner's OK before writing code (:86).

4. RENDER THE FRAME: the page exposes window.DUR, window.render(t), window.READY (TECHNIQUE.md:35-43). render(t) must be deterministic and stateless so any frame can be rendered alone in any order (:65). Lemo's tool loads the page in headless Chromium at 1920x1080, calls render(t) and saves a JPEG at quality 92 (core/render/still.mjs:18-23, page.mjs:43); a page error or a failed script load aborts with exit 1 (page.mjs:53-65). The original already satisfies this contract in spirit (scene = pure function of frame, FPS 30, DURATION 900 -> DUR = 30 s, t = frame/30).

5. SELF-CHECK BEFORE SHOWING: compare the still against the written style rules and fix what is off, once (DIRECTOR.md:61, MY-STYLES.md:101). Also run the six common failures list (DIRECTOR.md:104-111): subject too small or pushed to the edge; too dark or same-colour-on-same-colour; text covering the subject; an action too fast to read; blank frames in transitions; a timed effect that stops tracking after the camera moves. Framing rule: at key moments the subject fills at least a third of frame height with a readable silhouette (:92).

6. SIDE-BY-SIDE WITH THE BASE: render the same frame a second time with the base's settings and tile the two, base on the LEFT, new on the RIGHT, so only the intended changes differ (MY-STYLES.md:103; files styleframe.jpg and styleframe-vs-base.jpg, :22-23; tiling by core/render/sheet.py). For this job: base = original scene at the same frame, right = remake.

7. HUMAN GATE: show the frame and wait (MY-STYLES.md:106; MAINTAINING.md:33). If the owner wants more, update the style sheet and CHANGES table and render again. After two rounds of notes without success, say so and propose a different base instead of grinding. Note: lemo's default film workflow does NOT stop for approval unless a storyboard was requested (AGENTS.md:77); this project needs the stop, so follow the MY-STYLES/MAINTAINING gate.

8. OPTIONAL STORYBOARD SHEET: 6-9 key shots rendered with the real code, tiled into one sheet with shot number, framing and duration under each, sent with a note on what the director is least sure about (DIRECTOR.md:65). Useful here as a one-image overview of all five scenes once two or three are done, to catch colour drift between scenes.

9. MOTION AFTER APPROVAL: one timeline object is the single source of truth for all cue times (TECHNIQUE.md:84-91). Camera and light move on every frame; a stepped camera reads as lag (:67). Every subject-following effect goes through one world-to-screen function (:68; failure listed at DIRECTOR.md:111). Performance rules (DIRECTOR.md:94-102): anticipation, action, follow-through on every meaningful move; blend poses with keyframes and easing, never switch a pose inside an if; a rolling object turns by distance / radius (truck wheels); step through key actions at 0.2 s intervals, enlarged. Camera (DIRECTOR.md:87-92): each move needs a reason, design transitions inside the medium rather than default fades or hard cuts. Rhythm/reading time (:75-85): vary pace, give one breath; after text finishes animating in hold it roughly CJK characters / 4.5 + 1.5 s, a title card at least 4 s.

10. VERIFY SHOTS (TECHNIQUE.md:124-129, DIRECTOR.md:113-122): (a) contact sheets, a frame every 1-2 s over the whole film, tiled, at least two full passes; (b) frame strips at 0.2 s for every key action (for this job: forklift hand-offs, dock loading, truck starts/stops, every scene-to-scene move); (c) on the recorded file: blackdetect for blank frames, no NaN frames; (d) one viewing at full speed; (e) one fix round: fix everything the review found in one pass, re-check once, anything bigger is reported to the owner in one line; (f) every map frame checked enlarged against the map rules; (g) optional machine check of on-screen text hold time via window.TEXTS(t) + readcheck.mjs (exit 0 pass, 1 too short, 2 cannot check).

skills.whatItOffersHere:
A UI design skill, but three parts transfer well to a hero film: (1) a dependency-free screenshot/sequence tool, (2) an independent visual review protocol with a written rubric, (3) motion-feel rules.

(1) scripts/shoot.mjs (2151 lines) + scripts/chrome.mjs: uses only Node built-ins and the installed Chrome/Edge (found at C:/Program Files/Google/Chrome/Application/chrome.exe and the Edge path) in headless mode with a throw-away profile (chrome.mjs:80-82); serves the page itself on 127.0.0.1; needs Node 22+ (machine has v24.16.0); no npm packages, no downloads. It writes named PNGs plus report.json with checks for console errors, horizontal overflow, failed images, text contrast, text under 11 px and content stuck transparent on first screen (references/tools.md:80-87). Useful flags (shoot.mjs:15-56): --size desktop,mobile (1440x900 and 390x844) or WxH, --frames N (2-120 evenly spaced, time-stamped frames in one sequence image, no video), --entry (capture first-load entrance), --steps "click ...; wait 300", --selector, --sheet, --mask (text hidden, to judge pure composition), --thumb (half-resolution quick look), --mark, --stitch a.png --label ... --stitch b.png --label ... (side-by-side image without a page), --dry-run, --record (video, needs ffmpeg; only when full-speed feel must be judged).

(2) Independent review: references/visual-review.md (who gets what) + references/reviewer-manual.md (rubric). The main agent hands a fresh reviewer the current screenshots, the task, the constraints and the one-sentence design intent - and NOT the source code, self-justifications or earlier scores (visual-review.md:19-22). Reviewer steps that fit a hero film (reviewer-manual.md): three-second test on a 480 px-wide thumbnail and again with text masked, write down what is seen first (line 18); veto if the subject of the frame cannot be named after three seconds (16); the swap-the-company-name test - would the frame still fit another company (15); polish check at 200% for the roughest element, alignment and consistency (29); design check - is the main subject visible in the thumbnail, where is it still default-looking (30); motion check - what moves mechanically (constant speed, everything moving separately) and which move deserves real weight, described as action + physical object rather than adjectives (31); output = short numbered checklist (location: symptom -> result that can be verified), max 5 problems + max 5 improvements, one line of what must be preserved (43-46). Handling feedback: fix top-down, do not sand off the preserved item, stop if opinions ping-pong without visible gain (visual-review.md:31-35).

(3) Motion feel, references/motion.md: name the feel as action + physical object and derive spring stiffness/damping from it (table 27-34: click 350-400/10-15, slide-in 250-300/20-25, flow 150-200/30-40, slam 400-500/5-10, bounce 300/8, float 100/25); heavy materials get click/slam, light ones float/flow (36); overshoot scales with area - whole-frame or panel-sized things at most 1-2%, small badges 10-20% (38); a spring can be sampled into 20-30 points for a CSS linear() curve (40); one action propagates along one path - the lead moves first, affected things follow 40-80 ms later and smaller (44-50); leaving is faster than entering, about 60-70% of the enter time (72); reduced motion: every state goes straight to its final position with nothing missing (112); test at normal speed, then backwards, then rapid repeated input - no ghosting, jumps, things flying in from odd places or stuck mid-state; report frame rate only if actually measured (116).

Also useful: references/design-direction.md:137-162 the direction card (fields worth copying into the Sanpou style sheet: north-star sentence; colour as hex + role with at least three layers plus one sentence saying what in the product it comes from; motion written as sound-word + object; the one or two memory points; what is deliberately given up), :115-123 colour rule (colour comes first from the brand's own assets and real objects, write the category's default palette and the benchmark's palette first, then choose away from them); references/media.md:38 quality bar for vector objects - draw three layers of detail (lit outer volume, structural connectors, surface texture), never a thin single-colour icon; references/tools.md:76 an empty WebGL screenshot is not evidence, and frame sequences prove state changes but not full-speed feel; tools.md:78 when writing your own Playwright script add --use-mock-keychain --password-store=basic and a temporary profile; references/workdir.md process files go in .oil-ui/<task>/ with its own .gitignore unless the project has its own convention (this project should use its own folders).

skills.whatItOffersHere:
A de-AI-look checklist and a five-line direction format; it is a UI clean-up skill, so use it as an audit lens on the art and on the hero overlay, not as a workflow.

- Direction in five lines before touching anything (SKILL.md:54-66): Product (one plain sentence), Character (two or three concrete words; generic words such as clean/modern/premium are banned), World (the place or material the product belongs to - it sets neutral tint, accent and visual), Moments (the one or two places that get rich colour and detail), Signature (one small detail only this product would have, used consistently; the skill's own illustration for a delivery product is a route line, line 62, which matches the project's "one route line threading through the scenes"). Then show the direction and stop for the owner's answer (step 4, line 44).
- What good looks like (SKILL.md:23-29): one bright element per screen, quiet chrome around it, the visual explainable in one sentence, text placed on calm space that was left for it, objects that look like real things with weight, light and shadow. Applied here: the scene is the bright element, the hero overlay (navy copy on pale wash) must stay quiet, and each scene needs a calm sky/ground area where the copy sits.
- references/signs.md as an audit list for the illustration itself: colour glows and coloured shadows (line 9), radial colour washes and blurred blobs behind content (10), every element highlighted so nothing leads (13), floating blobs/orbs/grids/glowing lines (68, 77), an image that does not blend into the page - hard edge, different base colour (80); plus the "template look" test (92-99: would it fit another company if the name were swapped). This is the guard against the Motion film's dark-cyber weakness and against over-using glow/bloom if Canvas/WebGL is chosen.
- references/visuals.md:25: the style family closest to the goal is painted background art - calm sky/landscape with one subject, crisp clouds, soft light, open sky left for text; :33-38 what fails: baked-in grain/mottle textures (add texture in code if at all), a print/filter style on one image while the rest is plain, several subjects in one picture, purple-blue glossy abstractions; :77 match image edges to the page background or fade them with a mask - a hard rectangle of a different colour is a tell (relevant to how the stage meets the page).
